mcqs.q: A colloid is a mixture that is:
opts: Intermediate between a suspension and a solution (particles 1–1000 nm), e.g. milk
mcqs.explain: Colloids (1–1000 nm) lie between solutions (0.01–1 nm) and suspensions (>1000 nm).

mcqs.q: A colloidal system whose dispersion medium is water is called a:
mcqs.explain: When the dispersion medium is water, the colloid is a hydrocolloid (agar, alginate).

mcqs.q: The two physical forms of a hydrocolloid are:
mcqs.explain: Hydrocolloids exist as a sol (liquid) or a gel (jelly).

mcqs.q: A REVERSIBLE hydrocolloid changes sol ⇌ gel by:
mcqs.explain: Reversible = physical (temperature): heat gel → sol, cool sol → gel. Irreversible = chemical (sol → gel).

mcqs.q: The loss of water from a gel by evaporation or exudation is termed:
mcqs.explain: Syneresis = water loss; imbibition = water uptake. Both distort the impression.

mcqs.q: If a water-deficient gel is placed in contact with water, it absorbs water by:
mcqs.explain: Imbibition is water uptake by a gel; this is why a soaking-wet storage towel distorts alginate.

mcqs.q: Agar (ADA No. 11) is best described as a:
mcqs.explain: Agar is an organic hydrophilic colloid from seaweed — reversible and elastic (sol ⇌ gel with temperature).

mcqs.q: In the 3-chamber hydrocolloid conditioner, the first (liquefying) step is performed at:
mcqs.explain: Liquefy at 100°C ×10 min (gel→sol), store at 65°C, temper at 46°C ×3 min.

mcqs.q: Agar impressions use rim-lock trays because:
opts: Agar does not adhere to the tray, so beading/rim-lock mechanically retains it (with water cooling)
mcqs.explain: Rim-lock beading retains the non-adhering agar, and water circulation (18–21°C) gels it.

opts: An irreversible, elastic hydrocolloid — the most widely used dental impression material
mcqs.explain: Alginate is an irreversible elastic hydrocolloid from brown seaweed, and the most widely used impression material.

mcqs.q: The largest component (by weight) of alginate powder is:
mcqs.explain: Diatomaceous earth (~60%) is the filler; potassium alginate ~15% and calcium sulphate ~16% drive the set; sodium phosphate ~2% is the retarder.

mcqs.q: Alginate powder is best mixed using a:
opts: Vigorous figure-of-eight motion, swiping against the sides of a plaster bowl
Gentle circular stir in a metal cup
Single sweep with a wax knife
mcqs.explain: A vigorous figure-of-eight against the bowl dissolves all the alginate to a smooth, creamy, non-dripping mix.

mcqs.q: The recommended way to control alginate's gelation time is to alter the:
opts: Temperature of the mixing water (colder = longer, warmer = shorter)
mcqs.explain: Control set with water temperature; do NOT change the W/P ratio or mixing time (these harm properties).

mcqs.q: If an alginate impression must be stored before pouring, it should be:
opts: Kept in a damp (not soaking) towel or sealed bag for no more than one hour
Left dry on the bench overnight
mcqs.explain: Store ≤1 hour in a damp towel/sealed bag; a soaking-wet towel causes imbibition, and drying causes syneresis.

mcqs.q: Because alginate distorts on immersion, it is best disinfected by:
opts: Spraying and sealing in a bag for ~10 minutes
mcqs.explain: Alginate distorts if immersed, so spray-disinfect and seal ~10 min.

mcqs.q: A recognized USE of alginate is:
opts: Primary impressions for complete dentures and study/working casts
Final crown margins requiring the finest detail
mcqs.explain: Alginate is used for primary/complete-denture impressions, study and working casts, undercuts, high-saliva mouths and duplicating models.

saqs.q: Distinguish a suspension, a solution and a colloid by particle size, and define a hydrocolloid.
saqs.a: Suspension = heterogeneous, particles > 1000 nm, components separate (e.g. sand in water). Solution = homogeneous, particles 0.01–1 nm, stays mixed (e.g. salt in water). Colloid = intermediate, particles 1–1000 nm (e.g. milk). A hydrocolloid is a colloid whose dispersion medium is water (e.g. agar, alginate).

saqs.q: Define syneresis and imbibition and explain their clinical relevance.
saqs.a: Syneresis is the loss of water from a gel by evaporation or exudation; imbibition is the uptake of water by a water-deficient gel on contact with water. Both distort hydrocolloid impressions, so the impression should be poured promptly and, if stored, kept in a damp (not soaking) environment for no more than one hour.

saqs.q: Describe the conditioning of agar (the 3-chamber unit) and why rim-lock trays are used.
saqs.a: Agar is conditioned in a 3-chamber unit: (1) liquefy at 100°C for ~10 min to convert gel → sol, (2) store at 65°C, (3) temper at 46°C for ~3 min before loading. It is used in water-cooled rim-lock trays because agar does not adhere to the tray — the rim-lock beading retains it mechanically, and water circulated at 18–21°C for ~3 min gels it (sol → gel).

saqs.q: Give the two types of alginate with their working/setting times, and state how gelation time is controlled.
saqs.a: Type I (regular set): working time ~2 min, setting time 2–4.5 min. Type II (fast set): working time ~75 s, setting time 1–2 min (ideal gelation 2–3 min at 25°C). Gelation is controlled by the temperature of the mixing water — colder water lengthens and warmer water shortens the set — not by changing the water/powder ratio or the mixing time.

saqs.q: List two advantages and two disadvantages of alginate.
saqs.a: Advantages (any two): easy to mix/manipulate; dimensionally accurate if poured soon after removal; does not lose surface detail in wet mouths; wide range available; economical; records undercuts. Disadvantages (any two): does not flow well into areas the tray does not extend to; cannot be added to if faulty; liable to distort (must be poured promptly).
